name: RocksDB
summary: An embedded persistent key-value engine that uses an LSM design, write-ahead logging, column families, background compaction, and snapshot read boundaries.

features.name: Log-structured merge key-value storage
features.description: RocksDB is a persistent key-value store with a Log-Structured-Merge design, exposing a library API for embedded use and tuning trade-offs among write, read, and space amplification.
benefits: Supports high write throughput through sequential and batched updates
Makes storage amplification trade-offs explicit for workload tuning
costs: Reads may consult multiple levels or structures
Compaction consumes background I/O, CPU, and write bandwidth

features.name: Column-family state partitioning
features.description: The public DB API exposes named column-family descriptors and handles, and write, read, flush, and snapshot operations can be associated with a column family.
benefits: Partitions key-value state and configuration within one database
Provides handles that make the target state explicit at API boundaries
costs: Multiple families add lifecycle and recovery coordination
Compaction and flush behavior must be reasoned about per family and across shared logs

features.name: Write-ahead-log-backed write path
features.description: The public API exposes WriteBatch and WriteOptions, documents WAL synchronization boundaries, and the DB implementation contains WAL management and recovery paths before memtable flush and compaction work.
benefits: Provides a sequential recovery representation for recent writes
Allows write acknowledgement and WAL synchronization to be configured separately
costs: WAL retention and recovery add storage and startup work
Unsynchronized or indeterminate writes require explicit failure handling

features.name: Background flush and compaction
features.description: The RocksDB implementation schedules flush and compaction work in the background, moving mutable write state toward persistent sorted files and managing the resulting WAL and manifest boundaries.
benefits: Keeps foreground writes separate from much of the storage reorganization work
Controls read and space amplification through configurable compaction policy
costs: Background work competes with foreground reads and writes for resources
Compaction debt can increase latency and storage pressure

features.name: Sequence-bounded snapshot reads
features.description: RocksDB exposes snapshots as read views tied to a database sequence boundary, allowing a reader to observe a consistent view while later writes proceed.
benefits: Provides stable read boundaries for concurrent readers
Separates reader visibility from the current mutable write position
costs: Long-lived snapshots can retain versions and delay cleanup
Snapshot consistency does not by itself provide a multi-process transaction protocol

mathematical_views.question: How does a logical key-value map refine into mutable write state, WAL records, sorted files, and compaction generations?
assumptions: The logical map is compared at explicit sequence or recovery boundaries
Flush and compaction preserve the modeled key-value observations
Amplification and physical file layout are separate cost dimensions

mathematical_views.question: Which durable write sequence and database-file state reconstruct a valid logical database after restart?
assumptions: WAL records are replayed according to the configured recovery boundary
Manifest, column-family, and file transitions are represented explicitly
The model does not equate a successful write call with an fsynced record unless the options require it

mathematical_views.question: Which versions of keys are visible to a reader holding a snapshot sequence number?
assumptions: Writes have monotonically ordered database sequence numbers
A snapshot fixes the reader boundary while later writes remain outside it
Compaction is modeled as representation change that preserves required visible versions

benefits: Write-oriented persistent storage with tunable amplification
costs: Read and compaction amplification require workload-aware tuning

benefits: Named state partitions within one embedded database
Recoverable recent writes and configurable sync behavior
costs: WAL storage, replay, and failure-boundary complexity
Background resource pressure and compaction debt
Pinned versions and cleanup pressure for long-lived readers
